title: Layering every technique in RAG, one query at a time - David Karam, Pi Labs (fmr. Google Search)
talk_summary: A Google Search veteran lays out a 'quality engineering loop' for retrieval systems: baseline against a query set, do loss analysis, then apply the cheapest technique that fixes the observed failure, escalating only when simpler layers break. Techniques are ordered by difficulty/impact (in-memory context, BM25, embeddings, rerankers, custom embeddings, non-relevance signals, click signals, query fan-out, supplementary retrieval, distillation), with the core message that everything is empirical and driven by what your queries actually fail on.

takeaways.what_they_do: Baseline against a tiered query set (easy/medium/hard), then do a loss analysis of what's broken before picking any technique; only fix what the data shows is failing.
Rank candidate techniques by difficulty vs impact and only adopt the hard ones (custom embeddings, fine-tuning) when a simpler layer demonstrably fails.
takeaways.evidence_quote: complexity adjusted impact or you know stay lazy... always look at what's broken and if it's not broken don't fix it

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of letting the LLM form one big query, the system decomposes it into N narrow subqueries and fans them out, because the LLM can't be taught the backend's expectations via prompting alone.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you actually take more control of the actual orchestration so you take the big query and you make n smaller queries out of
takeaways.numbers: Google AI mode makes 15-20 queries per complex input

takeaways.technique: Supplementary retrieval / search more for recall
takeaways.what_they_do: When recall matters, deliberately retrieve more candidates/backends rather than optimizing for minimal calls; only trim when cost overload is the actual bottleneck.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when you're trying to get high call, you should always be searching more... just search more

takeaways.what_they_do: Relevance/semantic similarity is only a proxy; real ranking combines domain signals (price, merchant, popularity, click feedback) into a balanced score.
When the system understands a case well, show a high-promise UI; when it doesn't, degrade to a still-workable experience (show 10 options, let human choose) rather than pretending certainty.
takeaways.evidence_quote: gracefully degrade, gracefully upgrade depending on like the the level of your understanding
